cards.q: A dense layer maps 784 inputs to 128 neurons. How many parameters does it have, and what is the usual counting mistake?
cards.a: 784 x 128 + 128 = 100,480. The mistake is forgetting the 128 biases (giving 100,352). Batch size never changes the parameter count, and the input layer itself has no parameters.

cards.q: What does a 784 -> 1000 -> 10 network with no activation function equal, and what does the wide layer cost?
cards.a: Exactly one linear 784 -> 10 map, because two linear maps compose into one. It costs about 100 times more parameters for no extra power. The bend from the activation between layers is what you pay for.

cards.q: If the loss is a mean over N examples, what must the backward pass do, and what happens if you forget?
cards.a: Divide the gradient by N (the mean carries a 1/N). Forgetting it makes the effective learning rate N times bigger, so training explodes. Put the division in the very first line of the backward pass.

cards.q: What is the error at the output scores for sigmoid or softmax with cross-entropy, and how does it flow back through a layer?
cards.a: dz = p - y (prediction minus target). The weight gradient is dz times the layer input. The error passed back is dz times the weights, then multiplied by the activation slope of the previous layer.

cards.q: Why is feeding softmax probabilities into PyTorch `CrossEntropyLoss` a bug, and what do you feed instead?
cards.a: `CrossEntropyLoss` applies log-softmax itself and expects raw logits. Passing probabilities applies softmax twice. The model still trains, only worse, with no error message. Feed logits, and apply softmax only at inference.

cards.q: What is the difference between Adam with `weight_decay` and AdamW?
cards.a: In classic Adam the decay is added to the gradient and then rescaled by 1/sqrt(v), so it acts differently on each weight. AdamW decouples the decay and shrinks the weights directly. Use AdamW (the standard for transformers) when you want true weight decay.

cards.q: What should the first loss be for a fresh K-class classifier, and what does a much larger value suggest?
cards.a: About ln K, because predictions start near uniform: ln 2 = 0.693, ln 10 = 2.303. A far larger first loss suggests a too-large last layer or a label bug. Check this before tuning anything.

cards.q: Spot the bug: `loss.backward(); optimizer.zero_grad(); optimizer.step()`. What happens with plain SGD?
cards.a: `zero_grad()` wipes the gradients just before the step, so every update is zero and the loss never moves. Correct order: `zero_grad()`, `backward()`, `step()`.

cards.q: A fraud model reports 96% accuracy. What must you state before anyone trusts it?
cards.a: The majority-class baseline (96% if 96% of transactions are legitimate), then recall and precision on the rare class, measured on validation data with the production class balance.

cards.q: What are the four steps of the PyTorch training heartbeat, in order, and why does order matter?
cards.a: `opt.zero_grad()`, forward pass and loss, `loss.backward()`, `opt.step()`. Gradients accumulate into `.grad`, so skipping `zero_grad()` makes the next step use the sum of old and new gradients.

cards.q: About how much memory per parameter does fp32 training with Adam need, and what is excluded?
cards.a: About 16 bytes: 4 (weights) + 4 (gradients) + 8 (Adam's two moments). Activations are excluded and grow with batch size and sequence length. One billion parameters needs about 16 GB before activations.

cards.q: Convolution output size for input n, kernel k, padding p, stride s? Compute n=32,k=3,p=1,s=1 and n=28,k=5,p=0,s=1.
cards.a: out = floor((n + 2p - k)/s) + 1. First: (32 + 2 - 3)/1 + 1 = 32, so the size is kept. Second: (28 - 5)/1 + 1 = 24.

cards.q: Are CNNs translation invariant?
cards.a: No. Convolution is shift-equivariant: the feature map shifts when the input shifts. Invariance comes only from pooling and from training data that includes shifts. In one test an under-pooled CNN scored only 5.7% on shifted data.

cards.q: Rule of thumb for transfer learning: under 50 images per class, hundreds, or thousands?
cards.a: Under about 50 per class: linear probe, then compare with a small fine-tune. Hundreds with a similar domain: fine-tune the top blocks with discriminative rates. Thousands, or a very different domain (X-ray, satellite): fine-tune everything.

cards.q: Why give validation and test data no random augmentation, and why never rebalance the test set?
cards.a: Random augmentation makes the metric change from run to run, so scores are not comparable: use fixed resize and normalize only. The test set must keep real-world proportions, or precision and recall mislead.

cards.q: In NumPy, what does `np.uint8(250) + np.uint8(10)` give, and how do you avoid it in image code?
cards.a: It wraps around modulo 256 to 4, not 260. Convert to float first with `img.astype(np.float32)`, or use `np.clip`. Also: OpenCV is (H, W, C) in BGR order, PyTorch is (C, H, W).

cards.q: When does one global threshold (Otsu) fail, and what is the fix?
cards.a: With shadows or lighting gradients the histogram has no two clear clumps. Use adaptive thresholding or fix the lighting. Otsu picks the threshold that maximises the between-class variance w0*w1*(m0 - m1)^2.

cards.q: Two boxes have intersection area 600 and union area 2600. What is the IoU, and what threshold usually counts as a correct detection?
cards.a: IoU = intersection / union = 600/2600 = 0.2308 (union = A + B - intersection). The usual bar for a correct box is IoU of 0.5, so this pair does not match.

cards.q: Why is accuracy meaningless for a detector, and what should you report?
cards.a: Detection has no true negatives in the usual sense. Report mAP and say which one (mAP@0.5 or COCO mAP@[.5:.95]), plus precision and recall at your production threshold, and speed on your own hardware.

cards.q: Why must time-series windows be split by time, not shuffled?
cards.a: Neighbouring windows overlap, so a shuffled test window is almost identical to a training window and the score is falsely high. Split by time: train on the past, test on the future.

cards.q: Why can't you use a bidirectional RNN for forecasting?
cards.a: Its backward half reads the future. Training scores look wonderful, but at deployment the future is not available, so it fails. Use bidirectional models only when the whole sequence is known.

cards.q: Write scaled dot-product attention. Why divide by sqrt(d_k)?
cards.a: softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d_k)) V. Dot products grow with d_k, so without the scale softmax saturates into near one-hot rows and learning stalls. Dividing keeps the score standard deviation near 1.

cards.q: With d = 512 and H = 8 heads: what is d_h, the score shape, and the attention parameter count?
cards.a: d_h = 512/8 = 64. Scores have shape (B, H, T, T). Parameters stay 4d^2 (Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo) = 4 x 512^2 = 1,048,576 without biases, the same as one big head.

cards.q: GQA model: 32 layers, 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, d_h = 128, 4096 tokens, fp16. How big is the KV cache?
cards.a: 2 x layers x kv_heads x d_h x tokens x bytes = 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 4096 x 2 = 0.5 GiB. Using the 32 query heads would wrongly give 2 GiB: only key and value heads are cached.

cards.q: ViT on 224x224 images with 16x16 patches: how many tokens? What happens to attention cost if you halve the patch size?
cards.a: (224/16)^2 = 196 tokens. Halving the patch to 8 gives 28^2 = 784 tokens, 4 times as many, so attention cost (tokens^2) grows about 16 times.

cards.q: What loss does a CLIP-style model start at for a batch of N image-text pairs, and what is the loss computed over?
cards.a: Random guessing gives ln N (N = 8: 2.08). The loss is a symmetric cross-entropy over the N x N cosine-similarity table divided by temperature tau, with the matching pairs on the diagonal.

cards.q: Why do basic VAE images look blurry, and what is posterior collapse?
cards.a: The MSE loss averages over plausible outputs, which blurs images. Posterior collapse: the KL term falls to about 0 and the decoder ignores the code. Fix it by raising the weight on reconstruction or lowering beta.

cards.q: What does a diffusion network predict, and what must you pass it?
cards.a: It predicts the noise epsilon in x_t at one specific noise level, so it must be told the step t. Forgetting t, or sampling with a different schedule than in training, gives garbage images with no error.

cards.q: How much memory do 7 billion weights need in fp32, fp16 and int4?
cards.a: Parameters x bytes each: 7B x 4 = 28 GB in fp32, 7B x 2 = 14 GB in fp16, 7B x 0.5 = 3.5 GB in int4. This is weights only: activations and the KV cache come on top.

cards.q: In symmetric int8 quantization, how is the scale chosen and what is the maximum rounding error?
cards.a: s = max|w| / 127 and q = round(w / s). The largest rounding error is s/2. Outlier weights inflate s, so use per-channel scales.

quiz.q: A dense layer has 20 inputs and 64 neurons, and you feed batches of 32 examples. How many parameters does it have?
quiz.why: Parameters = inputs x neurons + biases = 20 x 64 + 64 = 1,344. The batch size never enters. 1,280 forgets the biases, 640 is 32 x 20 (confusing examples with neurons), and 2,048 is 32 x 64.

quiz.q: You build a house-price regression network and put a ReLU on the final layer. What goes wrong?
opts: Outputs are capped at 1, so every predicted price is squashed into a narrow range
ReLU makes the loss non-convex, so gradient descent can no longer be used at all
ReLU turns every earlier hidden layer into a linear layer, so the model cannot bend
Output is clipped at 0 and the slope is zero for z < 0, so rows stop teaching
quiz.why: A regression output should be linear. With ReLU the slope is exactly zero whenever z < 0, so those rows send no learning signal. The cap-at-1 answer describes a sigmoid, not a ReLU. Hidden layers are unaffected.

quiz.q: Your loss is a mean over a batch of N = 64 rows, but your backward pass sums the row gradients and never divides by N. What do you see?
opts: The effective learning rate is 64 times larger, so the loss can blow up
Nothing: the optimizer rescales the gradients automatically for each batch
Training is 64 times slower, but it still ends at exactly the same loss
Only the bias gradients are wrong, so accuracy drops slightly at the end
quiz.why: A mean loss carries 1/N. Without it every step is N times too big, which acts like a learning rate 64 times larger and often diverges. 'Slower' is backwards: oversized steps overshoot rather than crawl.

quiz.q: On Adam's very first update, one weight has gradient 100 and another has gradient 0.001. About how far does each move?
opts: Proportional to gradient size: the first weight moves 100,000 times further
Neither moves, because Adam's moment estimates start at zero at step one
Each moves by about the learning rate, since Adam divides by the gradient scale
The first moves 100 times further, because Adam only softens very large steps
quiz.why: Adam's step is lr * m_hat / (sqrt(v_hat) + eps). On step 1, m_hat is g and sqrt(v_hat) is |g|, so every weight moves by about lr, whatever its gradient size. Plain SGD is the one that scales with the gradient.

quiz.q: A 10-class model ends in a Softmax layer and is trained with `CrossEntropyLoss`. Accuracy rises but loss plateaus near 1.46. What is wrong?
opts: The learning rate is too high, so the loss cannot fall below that value
Ten classes is too many for cross-entropy, so MSE should be used instead
Softmax is applied twice: the loss already includes it, so output raw logits
BatchNorm is missing, so the logits are never normalised during training
quiz.why: `CrossEntropyLoss` includes log-softmax. A Softmax layer before it squashes outputs into 0..1, so the second softmax can never be confident: with 10 classes the best reachable loss is ln(1 + 9/e) = 1.46. A high learning rate would give a noisy or rising loss.

quiz.q: Gradient clipping is set to 0.03, but the model's typical gradient norm is about 0.2. What is happening?
opts: It fires on almost every step, so the clip value acts as the learning rate
Training is stable now, and clipping has changed nothing else about it
Clipping fires only on rare exploding steps, exactly as it was intended to
Gradients below 0.03 are scaled up to 0.03, which makes training faster
quiz.why: When clipping fires on nearly every step, every update has the same length, so the model is effectively doing normalised gradient descent with the clip value as step size. Log how often clipping fires.

quiz.q: You call `backward()` twice in a row without `zero_grad()`. What is in `.grad` afterwards?
opts: Only the second gradient, which overwrites the first one
The average of the two gradients, since both are valid estimates
Nothing: PyTorch raises an error on any second backward call
The sum of both gradients, because gradients accumulate in .grad
quiz.why: PyTorch adds new gradients to the old ones (the same as `+=`), so the update uses both. That is why you clear them each step. Overwriting is the tempting guess, but it is not how `.grad` works.

quiz.q: A 224 x 224 image goes through one conv with kernel 7, stride 2, padding 3. What is the output height and width?
quiz.why: out = floor((224 + 6 - 7)/2) + 1 = floor(111.5) + 1 = 112. 113 comes from rounding up instead of flooring, 111 forgets the +1, and 224 ignores the stride.

quiz.q: A depthwise-separable network has far fewer parameters than a standard CNN with equal accuracy. A teammate says it will be faster on your device. What is the right reply?
opts: Yes: fewer parameters always means lower latency on any device you use
No: depthwise convolutions are always slower than the standard ones on any device
Not necessarily: depthwise layers are memory-heavy; time it on your device
Only FLOPs matter, so count them and skip the timing test
quiz.why: Parameter count is not speed. Depthwise layers use memory heavily, and on some hardware that dominates. Measure time per prediction on the device you will ship on. 'Always slower' overcorrects: it depends on the hardware.

quiz.q: After unfreezing the backbone, validation accuracy falls. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The backbone learning rate is too high, causing catastrophic forgetting
The head learning rate is too small, so the new classes are learned slowly
There are too many classes, which always hurts fine-tuning accuracy
The BatchNorm layers have not seen enough data to settle in yet
quiz.why: A backbone learning rate that is too high overwrites the pretrained features (catastrophic forgetting), so validation accuracy drops after unfreezing. Fine-tune with a rate 10 to 100 times smaller than the head's.

quiz.q: Which grey-scale conversion matches the standard luma weights for R, G, B?
quiz.why: Luma weights are 0.299 for red, 0.587 for green, 0.114 for blue. The third option is the same weights applied in BGR order, the classic OpenCV mix-up. A plain average ignores that the eye is most sensitive to green.

quiz.q: Model A reports mAP 0.62 (mAP@0.5). Model B reports 0.48 (mAP@[.5:.95]). Which model is better?
opts: A is better, because its mAP is larger and mAP means the same everywhere
Cannot say: the metrics differ, so recompute both under the same one
B is better, because the stricter metric is always more accurate
They are equal, because both numbers are called mAP in the papers
quiz.why: mAP@[.5:.95] averages over stricter IoU thresholds and is always at most mAP@0.5 on the same detections, so the numbers are not comparable. Comparing them directly is the tempting mistake.

quiz.q: Why can an LSTM remember longer than a plain RNN?
opts: Its cell state is multiplied only by forget gates, so it can stay near 1
It has a larger hidden state, so more information simply fits inside
It uses ReLU instead of tanh, which removes saturation completely
Gradient clipping is built into every LSTM cell by design, so nothing vanishes
quiz.why: The cell state is a mostly additive memory path, multiplied only by forget gates. If f stays near 1, gradients survive many steps. Clipping is not built in, and it would only help exploding gradients anyway.

quiz.q: A transformer has neither positional encodings nor RoPE or ALiBi. What happens?
opts: Training stops with a shape error at the first attention layer
It works the same way, but attention costs twice as much
It acts as a bag of words and fails on order tasks, with no error
It only loses the ability to handle very long input sequences
quiz.why: Attention alone ignores order, so the model sees the tokens as a set. Everything runs, and quality quietly suffers on tasks where order matters. Long-input limits are a different issue.

quiz.q: You take softmax over the query axis instead of the key axis in attention. What do you observe?
opts: A shape error appears at the matrix multiply that follows the softmax
The loss becomes nan from the very first training step
Slightly lower accuracy, but the attention rows still sum to 1
No error and shapes match, but rows do not sum to 1: a silent bug
quiz.why: Softmax must normalise over the keys so each row of weights sums to 1. Over the wrong axis everything runs and the shapes match, which hides the bug. Print `weights.sum(-1)` and check it is all 1.

quiz.q: You train a ViT from scratch on 10,000 images and it loses to a ResNet. What is the best conclusion?
opts: Transformers are simply worse than CNNs for every image task
Expected: ViTs need much data or a pretrained start, so fine-tune one
Raise the patch size to 64 so that each token sees much more of the image
Remove the positional embeddings to make the model simpler to train
quiz.why: ViTs lack the built-in locality of CNNs, so with small data they usually lose. The fix is a pretrained ViT, not abandoning transformers. Larger patches would reduce detail, and positions are needed.

quiz.q: A GAN's generator loss keeps falling during training. What can you conclude?
opts: Nothing yet: the discriminator may be weaker, so check samples and FID
The generator is steadily improving, so training is going well overall
Training is converging, so you can stop and keep the current model now
FID must be falling as well, because the two always move together
quiz.why: In a two-player game a falling generator loss can mean the discriminator got worse. Judge by sample quality, diversity and FID, and save sample grids often. Loss curves are not a progress bar here.

quiz.q: You move training from 1 GPU to 4 GPUs, keeping a per-GPU batch of 32 and the same learning rate. What changed?
opts: Nothing: data parallel training is exactly equivalent to one GPU
Training is exactly 4 times faster, with no extra effort needed
The effective batch is 128, so re-tune the learning rate and warmup
The model is now 4 times larger because it is copied to each GPU
quiz.why: Data parallel averages gradients over all GPUs, so the effective batch is 32 x 4 = 128. Same learning rate and a bigger batch changes training behaviour. 4 GPUs rarely mean 4 times faster because of communication.
